serving.whatItIs: The infrastructure that runs the large language models your agent thinks with — engines and servers that load model weights and turn prompts into tokens, plus gateways that route requests across many models.
serving.problem: Hosted model APIs are convenient but cost per token, send your data to a third party, and lock you to one vendor's models and rate limits. Many teams need to run open-weight models on their own GPUs for cost, privacy, latency, or offline use.
serving.howItHelps: These tools load and serve models efficiently (batching, KV-cache, quantization) so you get high throughput on your own hardware, and gateways give you one OpenAI-compatible endpoint in front of any model so you can swap or load-balance without changing code.
serving.technical101: Inference engines like vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp implement paged attention, continuous batching and GGUF/quantized weights to maximize tokens/sec per GPU. Runners like Ollama and LocalAI wrap them in a simple local server; gateways like LiteLLM normalize 100+ providers behind the OpenAI API. Stacks like NVIDIA NeMo and TensorRT-LLM target large-scale, GPU-optimized deployment.

frameworks.whatItIs: Libraries for building a single agent in code — they wrap the model call in a loop that can use tools, parse structured output, and decide what to do next.
frameworks.problem: A raw model call just returns text. Turning that into an agent that can call functions, retry, validate output, and chain steps means writing a lot of plumbing (prompt templates, tool schemas, parsing, error handling) that's easy to get wrong.
frameworks.howItHelps: Frameworks give you batteries-included primitives — tool/function calling, structured outputs, the reasoning loop, memory hooks, streaming — so you describe the agent's tools and goal and the library runs the loop.
frameworks.technical101: Most expose an "agent" abstraction over chat completions with tool-calling: you register typed tools, the model emits tool calls, the framework executes them and feeds results back until the model produces a final answer. LangChain and LlamaIndex are broad ecosystems; Pydantic-AI and the OpenAI/Google SDKs emphasize typed, production-grade loops; DSPy compiles prompts as programs you optimize rather than hand-tune.

orchestration.whatItIs: Frameworks for coordinating multiple agents (or multiple steps) — assigning roles, passing work between them, and defining the control flow as a graph or workflow.
orchestration.problem: One agent with one prompt struggles with big, multi-stage tasks. Splitting work across specialized agents (planner, researcher, coder, reviewer) needs a way to route messages, share state, and control who runs when — otherwise you get loops, lost context, and chaos.
orchestration.howItHelps: These tools model the team: define agents and their roles, the hand-offs between them, and a graph/state machine that decides execution order, with shared memory and stopping conditions.
orchestration.technical101: Approaches range from conversational (AutoGen's agents that message each other) to role-based crews (CrewAI) to explicit state graphs (LangGraph) where nodes are steps and edges are transitions with checkpointing. The graph model gives you deterministic control, retries, and human-in-the-loop pauses that free-form agent chatter lacks.

autonomous.whatItIs: Goal-driven agents that take a high-level objective and try to plan and execute the whole thing on their own — breaking it into steps, running tools, and iterating until done.
autonomous.problem: Most agents do one bounded task. Some goals ("research X and write a report", "build this app") need open-ended planning, self-correction, and long-running execution that a single prompt can't cover.
autonomous.howItHelps: Autonomous agents add a plan-act-observe-reflect loop on top of a model: they generate a task list, execute tasks with tools, evaluate results, and replan — running for many steps with little supervision.
autonomous.technical101: Pioneered by AutoGPT and BabyAGI, these use the model as a planner that writes and reprioritizes a task queue, plus tools (web, files, code) to act. They're powerful demos but can loop, drift, or burn tokens, so treat most as reference designs and add guardrails — budgets, approvals, sandboxes — before production.

coding.whatItIs: Agents specialized for software — they read your repository, write and edit code, run commands and tests, and ship changes, usually inside an editor, terminal, or CI.
coding.problem: General chat models can suggest code but can't navigate a real codebase, run the build, see the errors, and iterate. Doing that by hand — copy-pasting between editor and chat — is slow and loses context.
coding.howItHelps: Coding agents connect the model to your files, shell, and tests so it can grep the repo, make multi-file edits, run the code, read failures, and fix them — turning "suggest a snippet" into "implement and verify a change".
coding.technical101: They combine repo indexing/retrieval, a tool loop (read/write file, run command, search), and a diff/patch format the model emits. SWE-agent and OpenHands target autonomous issue-fixing; Aider, Cline and Continue integrate with your editor/terminal for pair-programming. Quality hinges on test feedback and how well the agent grounds edits in the actual code.

skills.whatItIs: Packaged, reusable "skills" — prompt + tools + instructions for a specific capability — and the opinionated harnesses and registries that let an agent load many of them on demand.
skills.problem: Re-teaching an agent the same procedure (how to open a PR, run research, format a doc) in every project is wasteful, and giant prompts bloat context. Teams want to share proven agent behaviors like libraries.
skills.howItHelps: Skills externalize behavior into small, named units the agent discovers and loads only when relevant, so you compose capabilities instead of hand-writing each one — and version and share them across projects.
skills.technical101: A skill is typically a folder with a description, instructions, and optional scripts/tools; the harness indexes them and injects the right one based on the task, keeping context small. Anthropic's Skills define the format; gstack, superpowers and mattpocock/skills are opinionated collections and harnesses for coding agents like Claude Code.

sandboxes.whatItIs: Isolated execution environments — microVMs and sandboxes — where an agent can run code, install packages, and use a shell without touching your machine or production.
sandboxes.problem: Agents that execute model-generated code are a security risk: that code can delete files, exfiltrate secrets, or run forever. You need to run it somewhere disposable and contained, with hard limits.
sandboxes.howItHelps: These give each agent run a fresh, locked-down box — filesystem, network, CPU/memory limits, fast startup and teardown — so untrusted code runs safely and reproducibly, then is thrown away.
sandboxes.technical101: MicroVMs like Firecracker boot a minimal hardware-virtualized guest in ~100ms — stronger isolation than containers at near-container speed. E2B, microsandbox and agent-sandbox package this as code-interpreter/agent runtimes with SDKs; the tradeoff is isolation strength versus startup latency and resource overhead.

computer-use.whatItIs: Agents that operate a real browser, GUI, or desktop the way a person does — seeing the screen and clicking, typing, and navigating.
computer-use.problem: Lots of software has no API. To book a flight, fill a portal, or test a web app, an agent must drive the actual interface, which means perceiving a screen and producing mouse/keyboard actions reliably.
computer-use.howItHelps: These tools give the model eyes and hands: they screenshot or read the accessibility tree, let the model decide the next action, and execute clicks and keystrokes — automating any app that has a UI.
computer-use.technical101: Two main approaches: DOM/accessibility-driven (browser-use, Playwright-based) which read structured page elements, and vision-driven (OmniParser, UI-TARS) which parse pixels into clickable regions for screen/OS control. Reliability comes from grounding each action to the right element and recovering when the UI changes.

memory-rag.whatItIs: Systems that give an agent long-term memory and retrieval over your own data — vector stores, memory layers, and RAG pipelines that fetch relevant facts at query time.
memory-rag.problem: Models have a fixed context window and no memory between sessions, and they don't know your private or up-to-date data. Stuffing everything into the prompt is impossible and expensive.
memory-rag.howItHelps: These store knowledge and past interactions outside the model and retrieve just the relevant pieces to ground each response — so the agent "remembers" users and answers from your documents instead of hallucinating.
memory-rag.technical101: RAG embeds your data into vectors, stores them in a database (Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma), and at query time retrieves the nearest chunks to add to the prompt. Memory layers (mem0, Zep, Letta) add summarization, user/session memory, and knowledge graphs so relevant context persists and is recalled across turns.

data.whatItIs: Tools that turn messy, real-world inputs — PDFs, Office docs, HTML, scans — into clean, structured text and chunks an agent or RAG system can actually use.
data.problem: Your knowledge lives in formats models can't read well: complex PDFs, tables, slide decks, images, websites. Feeding raw bytes in produces garbage; you need faithful extraction first.
data.howItHelps: These parse and normalize documents — layout, tables, headings, OCR — into markdown/JSON, and crawl and clean web pages, so the downstream agent gets accurate, well-segmented content.
data.technical101: Converters like markitdown and docling preserve document structure (headings, tables, reading order) and OCR scans; unstructured and loaders split content into typed elements; web tools like Firecrawl and Jina Reader render and strip pages to LLM-friendly markdown. Extraction quality and chunking strategy directly determine RAG accuracy.

protocols.whatItIs: Open standards and servers that connect agents to external tools and to each other — most notably the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) protocols.
protocols.problem: Every tool integration used to be bespoke glue code, and every framework reinvented it. Without a standard, tools aren't portable across agents and agents can't interoperate.
protocols.howItHelps: A shared protocol lets any compliant agent discover and call any compliant tool, server, or other agent, so integrations are written once and reused everywhere — like a USB port for AI tools.
protocols.technical101: MCP defines a client-server spec where servers expose tools, resources, and prompts over a standard transport that any MCP client (Claude, IDEs, frameworks) can use. A2A standardizes agent-to-agent messaging and capability discovery. The payoff is a growing marketplace of reusable servers instead of N×M custom integrations.

observability.whatItIs: Tooling to see and measure what your agent actually did — tracing each step and LLM call, evaluating output quality, and monitoring cost, latency, and errors in dev and production.
observability.problem: Agents are non-deterministic and multi-step, so when they give a wrong or expensive answer it's hard to know which prompt, tool, or step caused it. You can't improve what you can't measure.
observability.howItHelps: These capture full traces of prompts, tool calls, and responses, let you score outputs with evals/test sets, and dashboard cost, latency, and failures — so you can debug regressions and prove quality before shipping.
observability.technical101: Tracing tools (Langfuse, Phoenix, OpenLLMetry) instrument each LLM/tool span, often via OpenTelemetry, with token and cost accounting. Eval frameworks (DeepEval and others) run datasets through your agent and grade with metrics or LLM-as-judge. Together they form the observe-evaluate-improve loop for non-deterministic systems.

runtimes.whatItIs: Low-code/no-code builders and hosting platforms that let you assemble, deploy, and run agents and workflows with minimal coding — often a visual canvas plus integrations.
runtimes.problem: Not every team wants to write and operate agent code. Building a chatbot or workflow from scratch — wiring models, tools, memory, and a UI, then hosting it — is a lot of undifferentiated work.
runtimes.howItHelps: These provide drag-and-drop flow builders, prebuilt connectors, and managed hosting so non-engineers (and engineers in a hurry) can ship an agent or automation fast.
runtimes.technical101: Platforms like Flowise, Langflow and Dify expose nodes — models, retrievers, tools, logic — on a visual graph that compiles to a runnable app with an API/UI; n8n and Activepieces focus on workflow automation across SaaS. The tradeoff is speed and accessibility versus the flexibility and version control of code.

voice.whatItIs: Models and frameworks for the audio side of agents — speech-to-text (ASR) to hear, text-to-speech (TTS) to speak, and realtime pipelines for live voice conversations.
voice.problem: Many use cases — phone support, assistants, accessibility — need spoken interaction, which requires fast, accurate transcription, natural-sounding speech, and low end-to-end latency that's hard to stitch together yourself.
voice.howItHelps: ASR models turn audio into text the agent can reason over, TTS turns its replies into speech, and realtime frameworks handle streaming, turn-taking, and interruption so conversations feel natural.
voice.technical101: Whisper (and faster-whisper/WhisperX) are the de facto open ASR models; TTS engines like Coqui, Piper and Fish-Speech synthesize voices, some cloning from a sample. Orchestrators like LiveKit Agents and Pipecat wire mic→ASR→LLM→TTS→speaker with barge-in and sub-second latency for live calls.
